title: Beeck v. Aquaslide ’N’ Dive Corp. (1977)
summary: The manufacturer could amend its answer to deny making the slide after discovering that its earlier admission was mistaken.
notes:
The decision does not permit withdrawal of any admission as of right. It concerns leave to amend, the record supporting good faith, and the trial court’s management discretion.

Aquaslide's original admission of manufacture rested on inspections by three insurance investigators; its president and owner Carl Meyer later inspected the slide himself before his deposition and concluded it was a counterfeit, and the Eighth Circuit affirmed under Rule 15(a) because the plaintiffs had not shown bad faith and might still have remedies against the actual manufacturer.

sections.Parties: Beeck and his wife sued Aquaslide after he was injured using a water slide.
sections.Material Facts: Initial investigations, including examinations undertaken for insurers, led Aquaslide to admit that it manufactured the slide. Its president later inspected it and concluded that it was not an Aquaslide product. By then the limitations period created difficulty for a suit against another manufacturer. The plaintiffs opposed withdrawal of the admission because of that potential effect on their recovery.
sections.Procedural History: The district court allowed the amendment and ordered a separate trial on manufacture. The jury found that Aquaslide had not manufactured the slide. The Eighth Circuit upheld the procedural rulings.
sections.Issue: Did permitting withdrawal of the admission improperly prejudice the plaintiffs or reflect an abuse of discretion?
sections.Holding: No. The record supported a good-faith mistake, and the court acted within its discretion in allowing the amendment and separate trial.
sections.Reasoning: Rule 15’s liberal policy does not eliminate scrutiny of delay, bad faith, or prejudice. Here the initial position arose from apparently reliable investigations rather than a deliberate attempt to mislead. The later inspection supplied a reason to correct it. The possibility that the plaintiffs would face difficulty recovering from someone else was important, but did not require a defendant to remain bound to an erroneous admission where the relevant prejudice and alternatives had been considered. A separate trial allowed the disputed manufacture question to be determined without immediately trying all liability and damages issues.

learning.why: The manufacturer could amend its answer to deny making the slide after discovering that its earlier admission was mistaken.

topics.cp-amendment: The court permitted correction of an earlier admission after considering good faith and prejudice.
topics.cp-denials: The proposed amendment withdrew an admission that the defendant manufactured the product.
topics.cp-separate-trials: Separate adjudication of product identity could isolate a threshold factual dispute.
topics.cp-judicial-discretion: Beeck applies the amendment standard to a mistaken admission and examines prejudice, delay, and good faith rather than treating amendment as automatic.
topics.cp-frcp-15: The amendment was allowed under Rule 15(a)'s freely-given standard absent bad faith or prejudice.
topics.cp-limitations: The claimed prejudice was that the statute of limitations had run against the true manufacturer.
topics.cp-frcp-42: The district court ordered a separate Rule 42(b) trial on the manufacture issue.
